It became the band's last Billboard Hot 100 Top 20 hit (No. 18) and last UK Top 10 single (No. 9), and topped the Billboard Mainstream Rock chart for five weeks, marking both a commercial peak and a symbolic farewell to The Who's classic commercial dominance.

J. Jackson. The video's post-apocalyptic visual language — scavenged clothing, desolate industrial backdrops, women in rags — drew from the Mad Max aesthetic then saturating popular culture, anchoring Kiss's reinvention within a recognizable genre framework while signaling a harder, less theatrically costumed direction. The video marks the transition from the Casablanca-era theatrical Kiss to the Mercury Records hard-rock-oriented act.

Its moderate runtime (3:53), moderate editing pace, and legible aesthetic make it highly accessible for archival screening and educational use.

The video's 1991 MTV VMA win for International Viewer's Choice underscored its status as a genuine artifact of peak transnational pop culture.
